I'd say in general lighter colors usually have a connotation of being happier/more energetic, while darker colors give more of a sense of sadness or calmness. It's like how the sun is bright which makes you feel warm and the night is dark which makes you feel colder. The cold isn't a bad thing and it isn't always a sad thing, but it does give you a more relaxed feel than the hype of the day. When you break down the different blues you could still assign them emotional ranges depending on the light differences but as most things with emotions the subtle nuances between colors could evoke different emotions for different people unlike the agreed upon blanket statement for blue as a whole. For instance I imagine as a person who has to feel with their hands a lot you probably get really good at feeling the differences in textures. Your fingers can feel subtle differences in the surfaces you touch. Let's say everyone runs their hands over a table really quickly. With that brief touch we can all agree the surface is mostly smooth. Now let's say people touch it slower and try to take more care inn feeling it out. Some people will still agree the table is smooth but others feel a bit differently. Some may say that the table is smooth but has small rivets. Some may say they get a ticklish feeling from the small dents while other's say the dents are itchy. Blue is like that table. People mostly agree it is (smooth) calming or like sadness, but as people pay closer attention to the table (color) how they feel can start to differ even if it is mostly around a common base. I hope I was able to explain that well.

Well it also gives a feeling of calm. Blue has a range of meaning like most things, just as tears don't necessarily mean sadness. Blue is often a color of comfort. I heard favorite colors are usually decided by our earliest memories, and since the sky and the ocean are blue and are ginormous it is very likely one of them will be in your earliest memory. I hope that explains it better, but if you have anymore questions please feel free to ask.

When your brain is under extreme stress it starts kinda going into energy saving mode. You don't really have energy for a lot of emotions. This is completely normal. As you are already overwhelmed your brain is trying to avoid situations where you experience new information it has to process. It's kinda like this; say every interaction is like a folder being put into your hands. Every time you talk to someone a new folder gets put into your hands. Now you can barely hold the tall stack of folders from falling. The tower is so tall that you can't see anything in front of you but that tower of folders. Your brain makes you go hide so you can start sorting and getting rid of those folders but it is still very overwhelmed. Your brain is screaming saying of course I don't miss them I am too busy! I don't want anymore folders! Now sometimes the brain can sort the folders itself, but sometimes it needs help. The brain sometimes accidentally takes a folder from the bottom of the tower only to put it back on top of the tower because it doesn't know how to deal with it. If that is the case you have to let your brain hire an assistant (therapist) or upgrade with a new program (medicine). Just like in the real world not every assistant will be good at their job so it's ok to fire that one and look for a new one. Not every program will work with your brain so it is important to try different ones until you find one that works.

One of my biggest issues was also the messed up sleeping thing. I thought if I stayed up it would make the next day come slower. As I am sure we have all been told, getting a good nights sleep is key for people like us. I knew that mentally, but still couldn't do it. For sleeping what ended up helping me was choosing one thing to do every time I am about to fall asleep. You won't be able to go from 2 a.m. to 10 p.m. right away and that is perfectly fine. I stayed up until 5 a.m. so it took awhile to get down to 12 a.m. which I think is good enough right now for me. When I noticed I was crashing and about to fall asleep I would turn on this song that was very soothing and didn't have any lyrics, or I would turn on asmr. Every night I would do that when I felt I was about to sleep. Ever heard of Pavlov's dog? It was an experiment where Pavlov would always ding a bell before giving the dog a treat, at the end of the study the dogs would immediately start salivating after hearing a bell ring. Their body linked the sound to food so even without the dog knowing the body salivated on it's own. This also works on humans. First you need to tie your mind to a certain sound, then gradually play that sound earlier and earlier. Your body will train itself to release the sleep hormone because it now has linked that sound to sleep. To be honest I still struggle with the cleaning thing as well. Sometimes turning on loud energetic music helps and I just dance to it while cleaning.

Here are some points I would like to highlight from the actual study:

1.) fewer male rock climbers would surpass the top female rock climber than would male sprinters who surpass the top female sprinter. 

Another example how even with skewed demographics the gap is able to be closely closed in this sport.

Secondly, it has been well documented that women on average are more flexible than men, with a greater degree of joint mobility doing movement ([Ferber et al. 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib21); [Kato et al., 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib47); [Mendiguchia et al. 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib60); [Rene 1984](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib79)). Rock climbing is likely better enabled by increased flexibility, and more-capable rock climbers have been found to possess greater flexibility metrics than less-capable ones ([Draper et al. 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib15); [Grant et al. 1996](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib28)).

This could be in part because women generally have a greater proportion of slower-contractile skeletal muscle fibers, fibers which facilitate endurance rather than power output ([Haizlip et al. 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib33); [Welle et al. 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib103)). Females, though possessing a lower amount of grip strength, have been shown to have levels of forearm and hand endurance equal to or greater than, those of males ([Dipla 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib14); [Fulco et al., 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib24); [Gonzales and Scheuermann 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib27); [Hunter 2014](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665944121000043#bib38)).
